alt: A time line with the text in the middle. Exigence sits on the left and looks back or around at what provoked the writing; purpose sits on the right and looks forward to the effect on the audience. Two fill-in frames test each: “Because ___, the writer wrote” and “The writer wants the audience to ___”.
caption: If it completes “Because ___”, it is exigence; if it completes “wants the audience to ___”, it is purpose.

alt: Four boxes name the kinds of exigence: an event, a problem, a question or controversy, and a need or opportunity, each with examples. Below, a named exigence is stated in the text, while an implicit one must be inferred from clues such as dates and references.
caption: Every text has an exigence; when it is implicit, infer it and point to the clue.

after: ## Purpose: use a verb and a target
alt: Four purposes are built from a verb and a target: persuade the council to reverse a cut, warn residents of a hazard, reassure anxious parents, mobilise volunteers to act. A table contrasts weak purposes that name a topic with strong ones that name the effect on the audience.
caption: A weak purpose names a topic; a strong one names a verb and its effect on the audience.

alt: Three linked boxes: the exigence (a flood damages the village’s road) leads to the writer’s goal (residents report new cracks quickly so repairs can be prioritised), which leads to the choices (a short notice, the phone number first, plain language).
caption: Exigence, then goal, then the choices that will bring the goal about.

after: ## Worked example 1: separating cause and goal in a wartime essay
alt: Paine’s opening is quoted with three phrases marked. Steps 1 and 3 on the left find and write the exigence, the military crisis of late 1776. Steps 2 and 4 on the right find and write the purpose, to rally discouraged soldiers and citizens. Step 5 checks that the two point in different directions in time.
caption: The exigence already exists; the purpose is something the writer wants to happen.

after: ## Worked example 2: an original notice (written by Marlbridge)
alt: The Elm Court notice split into three parts. The sentence about the leak found on Monday is the exigence. The closure and the instruction not to park on Elm Road are the primary purpose, given the most space and direct language. The shuttle van and the thanks are a secondary purpose of reassurance, working through tone.
caption: Primary purposes get the most space and the most direct language; secondary purposes often work through tone.

after: ## Reading for exigence and purpose under exam conditions
alt: A schematic passage page with callouts: the source line can supply the exigence or context; the first paragraph often signals the exigence; the last paragraph often states what the writer wants; request verbs such as “please sign” signal an action purpose. A note warns not to stop at the topic.
caption: Source line, first paragraph, last paragraph and request verbs: the four places to look.
